newsitem.title: USA: Writer's widow attacks abuse reports.
newsitem.headline: Writer's widow attacks abuse reports.

text.p: Novelist Louise Erdrich, widow of writer Michael Dorris who committed suicide last week, on Friday criticised reports that Dorris had been under investigation for child sexual abuse.

But Erdich did not deny the reports, telling the New York Times it was a "private matter" and she wanted it keep it that way. The Times also quoted a friend as saying Dorris was anguished over the possibility that he might be charged.
"This information has been obtained from people who really don't care about the emotional health of my children," Erdrich said in a separate interview in the St. Paul Pioneer Press.

"Some reporters love writing people's lives into fairy tales. Others love ripping a fairy tale to bits," she said. "Michael Dorris was an extraordinary man and his loss is unspeakable, a grief to his many friends, his family, and to a whole world of readers who will never know the pleasure of his next book."
In the Times interview Friday, Erdich said she knew that Dorris was suicidal from the second year of their marriage.

The Times also quoted Doug Foster, a close friend of Dorris and a former editor of Mother Jones magazine, as saying: "The Michael I spoke with in the final weeks was bewildered and anguished. He could see no way out and said he couldn't bear the thought of being charged with such crimes. He was concerned about the effect on his childollaren, his mother, Louise and his work."

Minneapolis police confirmed this week that Dorris, 52, was the subject of a criminal investigation. Sources familiar with the case told Reuters the charges involved child sexual abuse and friends said the allegations arose out of his bitter divorce and child custody proceedings with Erdrich.
Dorris was found in a Concord, New Hampshire, motel room a week ago. Police said he died after swallowing pills and fastening a plastic bag over his head.
A court hearing will be held in Minneapolis next week on whether records pertaining to the investigation to which Dorris was subject should be sealed, as Erdich wants.
Dorris, an essayist, children's writer and novelist, was the author of "The Broken Cord," which won the 1989 National Book Critics Circle Award.
